pages.title: About the firm
pages.content:
Ledger & Co. was founded on a simple idea: business owners deserve advisors who explain, not advisors who impress. Twenty-seven years later the firm has grown to fourteen partners and senior advisors, and the idea has not changed.

People first, then spreadsheets

Every engagement is led by a partner who stays with it from the first meeting to the final handover. We keep teams small so that you always know who is working on your business.

What we believe

Plain language

If we cannot explain it in a sentence, we have not understood it yet.

Ownership

Our work is finished when your team can run it without us.

Independence

We take no commissions and sell no software. Our only product is advice.

Our offices

We work from two offices in the city: the original head office on Market Street and a riverside studio opened in 2026. Most of our clients are within an hour's travel, and we are happy to work on site.

posts.title: The thirteen-week cash flow forecast, explained
posts.excerpt: A rolling quarter of weekly cash, built from receipts and payments rather than accounting profit, is the most useful spreadsheet a growing business can keep.
posts.content:
Profit tells you whether the business works. Cash tells you whether it survives the next quarter. The thirteen-week forecast sits between the two: detailed enough to act on, short enough to stay honest, and refreshed every week so that surprises arrive early rather than on payroll day.

Why thirteen weeks

A quarter is long enough to see the seasonal dip, the annual insurance renewal and the tax payment that everyone forgot. It is short enough that every line can be tied to a real invoice, contract or payroll run. Beyond thirteen weeks, a forecast turns into a budget; shorter than that, and it becomes a bank statement.

What goes into it

  • Opening cash taken from the bank, not from the ledger.
  • Receipts by customer, using how they actually pay rather than their terms.
  • Payments grouped into payroll, suppliers, rent, tax and debt service.
  • Headroom: closing cash plus any undrawn facility, against a minimum you agree in advance.

Making it a habit

  1. Update actuals every Monday morning before anything else.
  2. Roll the window forward one week and add the new thirteenth week.
  3. Explain every variance larger than an agreed threshold in a single sentence.
  4. Share the one-page summary with the leadership team by Tuesday.

The first forecast is always wrong. The fourth one is the first that people start to trust.

Engagement notes, finance practice

If you only change one thing this quarter, start the forecast. Our team can build the first version with you in about a week, and then hand it over so your own people own it.

posts.title: Pricing without fear: a practical review for service firms
posts.excerpt: Most service firms under-price by habit, not by strategy. A structured review shows where value is being given away and how to change it calmly.
posts.content:
Pricing is the fastest lever on profit and the one leadership teams touch least. Prices drift for years because changing them feels risky, and because nobody owns the question. A short, structured review takes the fear out of it.

Start with the evidence

Before discussing new prices, look at what you already know: win rates by proposal size, discounts granted and by whom, hours overrun on fixed-fee work, and which clients pay late. Patterns appear quickly.

Change in small, visible steps

Raise prices for new clients first, then for renewals, and explain the change in terms of what clients receive. Give your team a short script and the authority to hold the line. Track win rates for two quarters before the next move.

Done well, a pricing review is not about charging more for the same work. It is about being paid properly for the work you already do well.

posts.title: What a good board pack looks like
posts.excerpt: Shorter, earlier and built around decisions: the board pack that directors actually read.
posts.content:
A board pack is a tool for decisions, not an archive of everything that happened last month. Yet many packs run to eighty pages, arrive the night before, and leave directors guessing which pages matter.

Lead with the decisions

The first page should list the decisions the board is being asked to make, each with a recommendation and the page where the evidence sits. Everything else supports those choices or belongs in an appendix.

Our checklist

  • Sent at least five working days before the meeting.
  • A one-page dashboard of no more than twelve measures, with trends.
  • Commentary that explains movements rather than repeating numbers.
  • Risks with named owners and dates, not adjectives.
  • An appendix for anything a director might want but does not need.

Directors notice the difference within one cycle. Meetings get shorter, questions get sharper, and management spends less time preparing slides and more time running the business.

posts.title: Running a supplier risk review in a week
posts.excerpt: Map who you depend on, score what could go wrong and agree three actions, all in five working days.
posts.content:
Most businesses discover their supplier risk the hard way: a single shipment late, a key component discontinued, a contractor that quietly closes. A focused one-week review will not remove every risk, but it will show you where the real exposure sits.

Days 1–2

List every supplier above a spend threshold, plus any you could not replace within a month regardless of spend. Note what they provide and who owns the relationship.

Days 3–4

Score each supplier on impact and likelihood of disruption. Check concentration: how much of a product depends on one source, one region or one route.

Day 5

Agree three actions with owners and dates. Typical ones are a second source, a longer contract or a small buffer stock.

Keep it proportionate

The goal is a short register that people use, not a binder. Revisit it each quarter and whenever a supplier changes ownership, prices or lead times.

We found that one specialist courier carried most of our urgent orders. Nobody had ever written that down.

Operations director, manufacturing client

posts.title: Five signals a business is ready to scale
posts.excerpt: Growth stresses every weak joint in a business. These five signals suggest the foundations are ready.
posts.content:
Scaling is not simply doing more of the same. It multiplies whatever is already there: good processes become a strength, and quiet workarounds become daily emergencies. Before you push for growth, check for these signals.

  1. Your unit economics hold at volume. Margins do not depend on the founder personally handling every sale.
  2. Cash conversion is predictable. You know how long it takes for a sale to become money in the bank.
  3. The management team can run a month without you. Decisions get made where the information is.
  4. Systems are boring. Month-end closes on time without heroics.
  5. You can say no. There is a clear picture of the customers and work you do not want.

If two or more are missing

That is not a reason to stop. It is a reason to fix the foundations first, usually over two or three quarters, so that growth adds value rather than strain.

posts.title: Hiring a finance lead: the questions we ask
posts.excerpt: The first senior finance hire shapes a company for years. Here are the questions that separate a good bookkeeper from a strategic partner.
posts.content:
For many growing companies the first finance lead is the most important hire after the founding team. Get it right and the business gains a partner who turns numbers into decisions. Get it wrong and the founder ends up checking every spreadsheet.

Questions worth asking

  • Tell us about a forecast you built that turned out to be wrong. What did you change?
  • How would you explain our gross margin to a new sales hire?
  • Which month-end task would you automate first, and why?
  • Describe a time you disagreed with a chief executive about spending.

Look for someone who asks about the business before they ask about the software.

Partner, Ledger & Co.

We help clients define the role, run a structured interview process and, where useful, provide an interim finance lead while the search runs.

posts.title: Plain-language ESG reporting for mid-sized firms
posts.excerpt: Customers and lenders increasingly ask about environmental and social measures. You can answer clearly without a large team.
posts.content:
Environmental, social and governance questions now arrive in tender forms, bank reviews and customer audits. For a mid-sized firm the challenge is rarely the measures themselves; it is collecting the data once and answering consistently.

A sensible starting set

Environment

  • Energy use by site
  • Business travel
  • Waste and recycling rates

Social

  • Staff turnover
  • Training hours
  • Health and safety incidents

Governance

  • Board composition
  • Policies in place
  • Supplier code of conduct

Start with measures you can already collect accurately, publish them once a year in plain language, and improve the data before expanding the list.

posts.title: Reading a balance sheet in ten minutes
posts.excerpt: A quick routine for non-financial managers: four questions that reveal how healthy a balance sheet really is.
posts.content:
Balance sheets look intimidating, but a manager can learn a great deal in ten minutes by asking four questions in order. None of them requires an accounting qualification.

  1. Can the business pay its bills? Compare current assets with current liabilities.
  2. Where is cash tied up? Look at receivables and inventory against the size of sales.
  3. How is it funded? Compare debt with equity and note when loans fall due.
  4. What changed? Read the comparison column; movements tell the story.

Write one sentence for each answer. Those four sentences are often more useful in a meeting than the statement itself.
